title: Nell and Tinker's Wobbly Cake Adventure
markdown:
Nell the nightjar had feathers the colour of a dusky evening, soft grey with a little sparkle, like faraway stars. Tinker the terrier was a bounce of fluffy fur, tail wagging like a metronome that had forgotten the rules. His ears went flop-flop-flop when fun was happening, which was most of the time.

They lived in a cottage that smelled of fresh bread and sunshine left to dry on the sill. Nell flitted at the windowpanes, counting clouds that might or might not be boats. Tinker chased his tail through the little rooms until the furniture learned to stand aside, then flopped, grinning, as if the race had been the point.

Today was extra. Today was Bedwyr Bear’s birthday, and Bedwyr lived on the far side of a stream that giggled and splashed through the meadow, the sort of water that made stepping-stones feel ambitious. Nell and Tinker had made him a cake in the morning hush: eggs counted, flour clouding Nell’s feathers, Tinker licking a bowl he had been asked not to. The finished cake was round, plump, frosting swirled sunset-pink and sky-blue, smooth as painted clouds. It smelled like a party that had not started yet. They packed it on the best plate, the one with the chip that faced the wall.

“We must get this to Bedwyr,” chirped Nell, voice quivering like a leaf. “He will be so happy.”

Tinker thumped the floor. “Ready. Adventure.”

If they dawdled, birthday wishes might float off down the giggle and never come back. Nell’s deep-down worry was wobble. She gazed at the icing. “What if it squishes? It needs to stay swirly.” She pictured tiny bird feet failing, the masterpiece going splat in the stream, pink and blue becoming water.

“I’ll hold the plate steady,” barked Tinker, brown eyes sure. “You tell me which way. I’m your steady paw.”

They tiptoed toward the stream, cake between them: Tinker’s sturdy paws underneath, Nell perched on the rim, beak nudging the balance. The stones were not merely wobbly. They were performing a jig with every splash, moss as slippery as a rainbow that had been rained on.

“First stone,” chirped Nell.

Plink. Tinker’s front paw found a large round mossy stone. It wiggled. Nell fluffed rigid. A big wiggle.

“Second stone,” sang Tinker, cheerful even so. This one wobbled more. Nell’s tummy somersaulted. She went still as a statue of twilight feathers. She imagined the icing spun from moonlight, melt-if-you-stare.

A puff of wind whooshed through the trees and the stones danced harder. Tinker’s floppy ears threatened the bubbly water. “Wobble-woo,” he yelped. The plate tilted. Nell flapped, a tiny blur, and chirped sharp: “Right foot. A little more left. Quick.”

The stone under her felt ready for a cartwheel. She thought of turning back. She shut her eyes for a fleeting second, a blur of worry, then opened them because a closed eye does not steer a cake.

She took a breath. “Third stone. A big beautiful one.” She looked at the cake, the wobble, and her own iridescent tail feather—the one that helped on windy days. Precious. Bedwyr’s smile, more so. Her beak trembled. She nudged the feather free. It drifted into the stream. The wind carried wet moss and rush. The feather was gone, swallowed, and she felt a strange empty lightness where it had been.

They hopped and wobbled, oh so carefully, each paw and each tiny bird foot. Nell the guide, sharp eyes, clear chirps: “Smaller step. Wait. Now.” Tinker the mover, dependable paws, ears flopping in time and then, when asked, not flopping. It felt like balancing on a giant bowl of jelly that had opinions about birthdays. Each step a tiny adventure. Mid-stream a minnow came up to inspect the pink swirl and decided against a taste. A water-skater wrote a note and hurried off. A fourth stone tried a disco; Nell counted Tinker’s toes aloud until the dance ended. Spray kissed the plate’s rim. Nell leaned her whole small weight the other way, twilight feathers fanned, and the swirl held.

One final hop. Tinker’s paws met the soft grassy bank. Nell fluttered beside him, wings buzzing. They looked down. The icing was still perfectly swirly. Not a droplet escaped. As smooth as the kitchen table.

“We did it,” barked Tinker, whole body a wag.

Nell felt warmth chase the leftover wobbles. She had not let the worry turn them around.

They trotted to Bedwyr Bear’s cozy burrow. Friends were already gathered. Surprise, they said, in the happy way of a chorus that has been practising.

Bedwyr’s fuzzy face lit when he saw the cake, like a tree that had remembered December. “Nell. Tinker. The most beautiful cake I have ever seen.” He gave them a huge gentle bear hug that squeezed the air out in the happiest way, then set the plate on a stump that had been waiting to be a table. Friends leaned in. Someone hummed. The first knife-cut showed the sponge still level, a small miracle after jelly-stones.

Nell watched him enjoy a big slice, pink and blue melting with a contented sigh. A crumb found Tinker’s whisker and was officially allowed to stay. She nudged Tinker with her beak, twilight feathers rustling. Later, walking home the long dry way around, a gust rustled the leaves and a branch swayed. A tiny echo of the stone-fear fluttered. She puffed her chest. “Just the wind playing a game.” Steady warmth, like the memory of Tinker’s paws on moss. The wind was the wind. She was Nell, a bird who could handle a jiggly dance, one feather lighter and the icing still intact, Bedwyr’s laugh still carrying across the giggle of the stream.
